Empirical Research Plan: Stock-Price Mispricing, Equity Dependence, and Investment  
(period 1980–1999 Compustat/CRSP panel)

-------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Heterogeneity-robust Instrumental Variables (panel 2SLS).

Rationale  
• The object of interest—the causal effect of non-fundamental stock-price
movement on real investment—is potentially confounded by simultaneity
(fundamentals drive both Q and investment) and by measurement error in Q.  
• A powerful, widely used proxy for mispricing is the firm’s subsequent
buy-and-hold stock return: if the price at t is “too high,” abnormal negative
returns will follow, and vice-versa. Future returns are, by construction,
predetermined with respect to the firm’s decisions at t, so they can serve as an
external instrument for the mispricing component of Q.  
• The IV framework lets us interact the endogenous regressor (mispricing)
with continuous or discrete indicators of equity-finance dependence,
recovering heterogeneous causal effects.

Alternative designs (DiD or RDD) are less natural here because there is no
cleanly timed, economy-wide “shock” to stock prices that differentially hits
high- vs. low-equity-dependent firms, nor a clear running variable with a
credible cutoff. An IV strategy that separately identifies the mispricing
component is therefore most appropriate.

-------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
-------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
M̂_it  ≡ Mispricing component of Tobin’s Q (unobserved). We proxy it with the
observed Q_it and purge fundamentals via IV.

Operationally we run investment on Q_it, but interpret only the part of Q_it
that is instrumented by FUTRET_it (defined below) as “treated.”

Instrument  
FUTRET_it  = cumulative three-year buy-and-hold stock return from t+1 through
t+3, inclusive of delist returns and net of the CRSP value-weighted market
return. A high positive FUTRET implies ex-ante undervaluation; a high negative
FUTRET implies overvaluation.

Treatment heterogeneity dimension  
Equity-Dependence Index (EDI_it). We use the standardized Kaplan-Zingales
equity-dependence score, augmented with (i) firm-age decile (young firms are
typically more equity reliant) and (ii) 3-year rolling industry cash-flow
volatility. “High-EDI” firms = top tercile; “Low-EDI” firms = bottom tercile.

Control group  
Low-EDI firms serve as the counterfactual for High-EDI firms. Both groups are
observed in every year, enabling within-year comparisons after we partial out
firm and year fixed effects.

Treatment timing  
Annual—defined at fiscal-year end t; investment in year t is the outcome, Q_it
is the endogenous regressor, FUTRET_it the instrument.

-------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Instrument relevance  
FUTRET_it is strongly correlated (negatively) with the mispricing component of
Q_it. This is testable; we expect a first-stage F-stat > 10.

A2. Exclusion (instrument exogeneity)  
Conditional on current fundamentals (cash flow, size, industry trends, year
FE, firm FE), FUTRET_it affects current investment only through its effect on
the contemporaneous stock price/Q_it. That is, managers cannot foresee the
exact three-year abnormal return pattern in a way that separately affects
current investment.

A3. No “feedback” from current investment to FUTRET_it within the 3-year
window that would violate exclusion. Given typical gestation lags of new
capital, any effect of today’s investment on stock returns should materialise
only gradually and is largely fundamental (captured in Q_it), not in the
abnormal component.

A4. Homogeneous monotonicity (LATE condition)  
For every firm-year, a higher FUTRET_it moves Q_it in the same direction
(outward shift in price). Reasonable because Q_it is a monotone transformation
of price.

A5. SUTVA / stable composition  
Investment of one firm does not mechanically influence another firm’s
instrument (its own FUTRET) beyond economy-wide controls captured in year FE.

Plausibility  
Given that FUTRET_it is determined after time t, simultaneity concerns are
small. Insider trading could in theory link future returns to current
information unknown to the econometrician, but controlling for contemporaneous
fundamentals, analyst forecast revisions, and industry-year shocks makes the
exclusion restriction plausible.

-------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
-------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Violation of Exclusion: Investment today may influence abnormal future
returns (e.g., if managers deliberately over-invest, later disappointing the
market).  
Mitigation: (i) include predicted future fundamentals via analyst forecasts and
ROE expectations; (ii) use the industry-adjusted component of FUTRET_it (firm
return minus industry return) to remove shared shocks; (iii) run placebo tests
using FUTRET_it,k where k = +4…+6 years—little relevance should remain.

T2. Measurement error / misclassification in EDI_it.  
Mitigation: Build three alternative equity-dependence measures—(a) pure KZ,
(b) Hadlock-Pierce SA index, (c) lagged cash-flow–dividend payout ratio—to show
qualitatively similar interaction results; report attenuated-bias bounds.

T3. Omitted trends (e.g., tech boom 1998-1999 both inflates stock prices and
alters investment for young, equity-heavy firms).  
Mitigation: interact year FE with 2-digit SIC dummies; include firm-specific
linear time trends; cluster standard errors two-way by firm and year.

-------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# -----------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -----------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast fixed-effects & IV
library(modelsummary)

# -----------------------------------------------
# 1. Data loading
# -----------------------------------------------
comp <- read_csv("compustat_clean.csv")   # contains fundamentals
crsp <- read_csv("crsp_returns.csv")      # contains returns

# merge on permno + fiscal year
df <- comp %>% 
  left_join(crsp, by = c("permno","fyear")) %>% 
  arrange(permno, fyear)

# -----------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
# -----------------------------------------------
df <- df %>% 
  group_by(permno) %>% 
  mutate(lag_assets = lag(at),
         investment_capx = capx / lag_assets,
         q = (mkvalt + at - ceq) / at,
         operating_cf = oibdp / lag_assets,
         # cumulative 3-yr forward raw and mkt-adj returns
         futret_raw = lead(ret, 1) * (1 + lead(ret, 2)) * (1 + lead(ret, 3)) - 1,
         futret_mkt = futret_raw - lead(mktvw_return,3),          # mkt-adj
         # Kaplan-Zingales style EDI (simplified example)
         kz = -1.002*cf/lk_assets + 0.283*qltdebt/lk_assets + 3.139*dividends/lk_assets - 39.368*cash/lk_assets - 1.315*age,
         edi = scale(kz) + scale(age) + scale(ind_cf_vol),        # additive score
         high_edi = (edi > quantile(edi, .67)),
         low_edi  = (edi < quantile(edi, .33))
  ) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  filter(!is.na(investment_capx), !is.na(q), !is.na(futret_mkt))

# -----------------------------------------------
# 3. Main IV regression
# -----------------------------------------------
# First: entire sample with continuous EDI interaction
iv_main <- feols(investment_capx ~ q*edi + operating_cf |
                 permno + fyear |                    # fixed effects
                 q ~ futret_mkt,                     # instrument set
                 data = df, cluster = "permno")

# Alternative: discrete high vs low
df_sub <- df %>% filter(high_edi | low_edi)

iv_discrete <- feols(investment_capx ~ q*high_edi + operating_cf |
                     permno + fyear |
                     q ~ futret_mkt,
                     data = df_sub,
                     cluster = "permno")

# -----------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: alternate instrument (industry-adj)
# -----------------------------------------------
df <- df %>%
  group_by(fyear, sic2 = substr(sic,1,2)) %>%
  mutate(ind_ret = mean(futret_raw, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(futret_indadj = futret_raw - ind_ret)

iv_robust <- feols(investment_capx ~ q*edi + operating_cf |
                   permno + fyear |
                   q ~ futret_indadj,
                   data = df,
                   cluster = "permno")

# -----------------------------------------------
# 5. Output
# -----------------------------------------------
modelsummary(list(Main = iv_main, HighLow = iv_discrete, IndAdj = iv_robust),
             statistic = "statistic", stars = TRUE)
```

-------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts that the sensitivity of investment to *mispricing* (i.e.,
instrumented Q) is larger for equity-dependent firms:

β_low      ≈ 0.05 – 0.10  (Semi-elasticity of investment w.r.t. Q)  
β_high     ≈ 0.10 – 0.20  
Difference β_high – β_low ≈ 0.05 – 0.10 (economically meaningful: a one-sd
valuation shock raises the investment-to-asset ratio by ~1 pp more in the
high-EDI group).

We also expect equity issuance to co-move with mispricing in the same
differential pattern.

-------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)
-------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (first-stage F > 10) .................. 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction plausible & tested via over-ID ....... 0.5  
C3: Monotonicity (sign of first stage uniform) ................. 1  
C4: No interference / SUTVA .................................... 1  
C5: No severe sample selection or attrition bias ............... 0.5  

Total (out of 5) = 4.0 → “generally credible, but exclusion still the
critical assumption.”

-------------------------------------------------------------
End of research plan
